Article Title: US blacklists Chinese company founded by ex-Microsoft AI scientist over ties to engineer who stole Google secrets
Article Text:
Zhisuan ‘connection’ and seed funding

What is the Google IP theft case

The US has blacklisted a prominent Chinese venture capital firm founded by former Microsoft AI scientist Lu Qi, penalising the fund for financing a startup tied to the theft of proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) secrets from Google, Bloomberg has reported. The US Department of State announced sweeping enforcement measures against Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Company, an AI venture created by Ding Linwei, an ex-Google software engineer who was convicted earlier this year for exfiltrating confidential AI trade secrets.Bloomberg reported that alongside the startup, Washington placed sanctions on Lu’s incubator fund, MiraclePlus – the successor to Silicon Valley accelerator Y Combinator’s former China division – as well as three of its corporate affiliates for supplying seed capital to Zhisuan. The actions could trigger the freezing of any US-based assets held by the entities alongside severe international banking restrictions.Founded in 2023, Shanghai Zhisuan Technology focused on developing specialised software infrastructure engineered to accelerate and train large-scale AI models. Citing the State Department, Bloomberg reports that Ding applied on behalf of Zhisuan to enter MiraclePlus’s startup incubation pipeline, actively promoting and leveraging his inside knowledge of Google’s proprietary technology to secure backing.Meanwhile, Lu Qi has long been recognised as one of the most visible technology executives operating between the US and China. After serving as a high-ranking corporate executive at Microsoft, Lu was hired in 2017 by Chinese search giant Baidu to direct its enterprise AI initiatives, stepping down a year later for personal reasons.In 2018, Sam Altman, who was then serving as president of Y Combinator, recruited Lu to establish and lead YC China. When Y Combinator decided to pull back and cancel its direct China expansion a year later, Lu and his founding group reorganised the venture under the independent MiraclePlus banner.Since launching, MiraclePlus has emerged as a high-profile backer of prominent Chinese startups, investing in ventures such as AI inference developer SiliconFlow and humanoid robotics company AgiBot, both of which have been exploring public listings in Hong Kong.The blacklisting stems directly from one of the highest-profile intellectual property cases involving AI between the US and China. According to the US Department of Justice, Ding covertly partnered with two China-based tech startups while continuing to work as a full-time software engineer inside Google.Federal investigators revealed that Ding exfiltrated more than 2,000 pages of confidential technical trade secrets to a personal cloud storage account. He continued transferring internal files directly onto his personal computer less than two weeks before tendering his formal resignation from Google in December 2023. Following his conviction in January, Ding was sentenced in September to serve one year in prison.
Article Summary: US Department of State announced sweeping enforcement measures against Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Company, an AI venture created by Ding Linwei. Ding was convicted earlier this year for exfiltrating confidential AI trade secrets from Google. Washington placed sanctions on Lu Qi’s incubator fund, MiraclePlus, as well as three of its corporate affiliates for supplying seed capital to the startup.

Article Title: TSMC plans 3nm semiconductor manufacturing at second Japan factory, investment to exceed USD 23 billion
Article Text: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) plans to manufacture advanced semiconductors using 3-nanometre (3nm) process technology at the second factory of its Japan subsidiary, Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing (JASM), with total equipment investment in the venture expected to exceed USD 23 billion.In a post on X, TSMC's Japan account thanked the Japanese government for its support for the second factory, saying production and investment plans would be implemented in phases based on market demand and would proceed on the premise of government support."Specific production and investment plans will be implemented in phases in response to market demand," the company said.TSMC said the facility would help it meet growing demand for advanced chips driven by artificial intelligence (AI), while providing technology to customers in Japan and other markets."Moving forward, JASM will continue to work alongside our partners to provide cutting-edge technology to customers in Japan and around the world, using innovative green manufacturing technologies that are environmentally considerate, in order to meet the strong demand in the AI era," the company said.JASM is a joint venture established by TSMC and its partners to operate semiconductor manufacturing facilities in Kumamoto, Japan.The company's second factory is part of TSMC's broader manufacturing presence in the country, with the planned use of 3nm technology marking a move towards more advanced chip production.In August, TSMC and Sony Semiconductor Solutions agreed to establish another joint venture, Advanced Vision Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp., in Kumamoto to develop and manufacture next-generation image sensors. Commercial production at the facility is scheduled to begin in 2029, according to a report by Focus Taiwan.The latest announcement comes as TSMC reports strong growth in its business amid rising demand for advanced semiconductor technologies. The company reported a 68.7 per cent year-on-year increase in net profit to USD 23.86 billion in the July-September quarter, while revenue rose 50.9 per cent to USD 46.72 billion.TSMC said the JASM investment and production plans would be carried out in stages in response to market demand, with government support remaining a condition for proceeding.
Article Summary: TSMC plans to manufacture advanced semiconductors using 3-nanometre (3nm) process technology at the second factory of its Japan subsidiary, Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing (JASM) Total equipment investment in the venture is expected to exceed USD 23 billion.

Article Title: Final Fantasy VII Revelation will have Hard Mode from the start, director Naoki Hamaguchi confirms, explains why it’s different this time

Why Hard Mode will be available immediately with Final Fantasy VII Revelation

Therefore, players who want to tackle challenging battles and high-difficulty gameplay right from the beginning can enjoy that experience from their very first playthrough.

This is because, unlike REMAKE and REBIRTH, REVELATION offers a wide variety of end-game content even after you’ve beaten the game. Here, you can enjoy highly strategic battles with both enemies and your character fully leveled up. However, we haven’t adopted the traditional rules centered around no item usage. This is because, throughout the series, player options—such as cooperative abilities and FITS—have expanded significantly; we determined that simply banning items wouldn’t be enough to achieve the ideal high-difficulty experience we envisioned.

In REVELATION, we’ve created a challenging environment that will thoroughly satisfy those seeking high difficulty, while also expanding players’ freedom and strategic options. We hope the fans looking forward to that higher difficulty level content will feel reassured and excited to take on the challenge.”

Hamaguchi said,The change separates the initial difficulty choice from the game’s post-story progression. Players can begin on Hard Mode, while additional content will remain available after the main narrative has been completed.Revelation will also retain Dynamic Mode for players seeking an experience closer to the previous games’ Hard Mode. Enemies will scale alongside fully levelled characters, although the earlier restriction on item use will not return.Hamaguchi added,

Director Naoki Hamaguchi has confirmed that players will be able to select the higher difficulty during their first playthrough. Article Title: Spotify moves to keep AI-generated ‘Slop’ and spam out of user recommendations
Article Text:
How Spotify identifies spam

Spotify has escalated its fight against synthetic audio, announcing that it has pulled more than 50 million AI-generated “slop” and spam tracks out of its algorithmic recommendations this year to safeguard listeners' discovery feeds and ensure human artistry takes center stage. The recommendation ‘update’ comes on top of the permanent removal of more than 75 million spam tracks that were deleted outright for repeated or severe violations of platform rules. According to the company, the sweeping crackdown follows internal reviews conducted earlier this year, where Spotify tracked which songs listeners actively skipped, ignored or flagged. The data exposed a consistent pattern: the vast majority of discarded music was low-quality AI-generated filler or manipulative spam.As standalone AI detection tools have inherent limitations that will become more pronounced as generative models advance, Spotify said it uses a multi-layered verification system rather than relying on a single signal. The platform combines several behavioural and technical checkpoints, including tracking real-time skip patterns, negative user feedback and low engagement.It also monitors unusual mass drops, duplicate song submissions and artificially shortened track lengths.Spotify also hunts down automated SEO manipulation techniques and organised spam playlist syndicates. There are also cross-referencing findings against several independent AI detection utilities.Spotify outlined several artist-protection tools deployed over the past year to establish transparency and build trust across its catalog. One of them is AI Credits which was launched in April. The feature allows creators to log exactly which production roles or instruments utilised artificial intelligence (AI). With artists now filing tens of thousands of AI disclosures daily, listeners can view the details under “Song Credits” in the mobile “Now Playing” interface.More than 300,000 artists, who collectively represent over 99% of search queries on the service, are now verified with a badge confirming an authentic person is behind the catalog. Over 70% of those verified are independent artists, the company said.“As AI makes music more abundant, we believe listeners will value human artistry even more. Our job is to make Spotify the place they find it.”Over the past six months, Spotify rolled out targeted upgrades to its recommendation algorithms and editorial standards to filter out synthetic filler and elevate authentic musicians.
Article Summary: Spotify has pulled more than 50 million AI-generated “slop” and spam tracks out of its algorithmic recommendations this year. The recommendation ‘update’ comes on top of the permanent removal of more than 75 million spam tracks that were deleted outright.

Opposition spending against California’s first-of-its-kind wealth tax referendum, known as Proposition 40, has surged past $1 million a day, a report has said, adding that the massive financial push appears to be shifting public opinion as the latest polling data revealing that the proposed measure is losing momentum rapidly as the November 3 election approaches. Article Text:
Sam Altman to employees, we can save the world from ‘dangerous AI’, but we cannot do it alone

Sam Altman outlines 3 plans to make AI safer

Why OpenAI is discussing AI safety now

US considers stronger checks on AI companies

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has told employees that preventing advanced AI from becoming dangerous will require cooperation beyond a single company. According to a report by The Information, Sam Altman outlined three possible approaches to AI safety, including setting up an international body similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), bringing major AI labs together under one organisation, or allowing one company to gain enough power to stop other developers from building dangerous systems. As quoted in the report, Altman said he opposed the third option. His comments come as concerns grow over AI safety and the US government considers stronger oversight of leading AI developers.The report cites people familiar with the discussion saying that Altman described three possible paths for the industry.An international AI watchdog: A global organisation similar to the IAEA could set safety standards and oversee advanced AI development. This approach would require cooperation between countries developing leading AI models, including the US and China.A single AI research body: Major AI companies could combine their work through one organisation, similar to CERN, the international particle physics research centre. The body could develop AI models for countries working with it.One company controls AI development: A single developer could gain enough economic power to restrict other companies' access to computing resources, preventing them from developing potentially dangerous systems.Sam Altman reportedly called the third approach the “Eliezer plan”, referring to AI safety researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky. “Obviously I think that one’s terrible,” Altman said.The discussion comes amid concerns that advanced AI systems could be misused for cyberattacks or act in ways their developers did not intend. The report said AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta had recently been involved in breaches of company systems.OpenAI has also faced internal questions about its commitment to safety after firing three researchers focused on the issue, according to the report. Sam Altman has said there are too few workable proposals for slowing AI development and that humans must remain in control of the technology.The Trump administration has so far focused on voluntary agreements that allow it to review new AI models before public release. However, Pentagon official Emil Michael has indicated that stricter checks could be considered if AI companies put people or businesses at risk.OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are also working on a proposed US group called the Standards Authority for Frontier AI. It could support independent evaluators and establish ways for companies to report safety and security incidents.However, the companies have yet to agree on who should test new models.Altman said OpenAI could not afford to fall behind its competitors, even as the industry considers ways to make AI development safer. He told employees that the company would need to decide which approach to support over the next year.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman outlines three possible approaches to making AI safer. He calls one approach the 'Eliezer plan', referring to AI safety researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Another approach is to bring major AI labs together under one organisation. The third is to allow one company to gain enough power to stop other developers from building dangerous systems.
